newsitem.title: USA: Lower heat prices possible next year--wholesalers.
newsitem.headline: Lower heat prices possible next year--wholesalers.

text.p: Next winter U.S. consumers are expected to pay less for heating oil after prices burned holes in their wallets this winter, according to fuel wholesalers and retailers.
Behind the price cool down is a surplus of heating oil inventory left by this winter's mild temperatures in the northeastern United States, the largest heating oil market in the world.
Heating oil wholesalers and retailers in the Northeast are quick to point out that next year's heating oil prices are still vulnerable to prolonged cold or political events disrupting crude supply.

But, at a conference this week sponsored by their trade group, the New England Fuel Institute, they said consumers should get a respite in their heating oil expense provided temperatures are seasonally normal next winter.

"It's a fair assessment that because of the mild winter we had, we should see prices soften next year," said Michael Stahler, sales representative for Bradford Oil, a mid-sized heating oil retailer in Vermont.
In fact, this winter was among the ten most mild winters in Boston since such records have been kept, said Mike Palmerino, meteorologist with independent forecaster Weather Services Corp.
"With winter being considered December, January, and February, this winter in the Northeast has been about four degrees above normal," said Palmerino.
The American Petroleum Institute said as of February 28, heating oil stocks in the Northeast were 1.3 million barrels over a year ago.

"The variable that leads one to think prices could moderate for next year is that we are in an a oversupply situation. That is creating a contango environment, which is allowing wholesalers to stock more oil," said Frank Sestito, vice president at Sprague Energy, a leading wholesaler in the Northeast.

The stock surplus is making the heating oil futures contract on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) for supply nearer in time less expensive than the later contract - a price relationship called "contango".
This encourages dealers to store even more heating oil and pay for storage with the more expensive supply later.

The 1995/1996 winter was prolonged and cold, leaving heating oil inventories bare at season's end. Refiners subsequently did not replenish supplies due to a "just-in-time" inventory strategy whereby they produce according to near-term demand.
By the time this winter was approaching, stocks had dwindled to record-low levels.

Due to concerns of a shortage, the price of NYMEX heating oil futures skyrocketed to a post-Gulf War high this fall of 76.75 cents a gallon, pushing retail heating oil prices in Massachusetts to a 10-year high of $1.15 a gallon in December.
After government concern sparked meetings between refiners and the then U.S. Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary, heating oil was produced at record rates.
Industry sources say refiners will be sure to meet demand in the future to avoid government intervention.
Indeed, one trader with a leading heating oil importer noted high heating oil production continued even when prices began to drop.

"It looks like stocks are building back to normal . . . . They (refiners) were producing when cash (actual) prices were six cents under the Merc (NYMEX price). It's because the government stepped in," the trader said.
Wholesalers also note more supply is on the way with the summer restart of Tosco Corp's 150,000 barrel-per-day refinery in Trainer, Pennsylvania.

"Clearly, there are two things that would lead to thinking that there will be softness in the market, that is the stronger inventory position we are in going out of the season, and the fact that the Trainer refinery is coming onstream," said Rick Trout, northeast distillate manager for Mobil Corp.
-- New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1620
